secondary, the Patriots threw `{python} BAL14[0]` passes and ran `{python} BAL14[1]` times, and won 35–31 (the game in
which they also confused Baltimore with legal formations that made eligible receivers look ineligible, the trick
[Formation Rules](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) explains). Eight days
later, in the AFC Championship Game against an Indianapolis defense that couldn't stop the run, they ran it
`{python} IND14[1]` times; LeGarrette Blount carried `{python} BLOUNT_N` times for `{python} BLOUNT_Y` yards and
`{python} BLOUNT_TD` touchdowns, and New England won 45–7.[^pbp-games] Same coach, same quarterback, same playbook
language, nearly opposite offenses.

Or look at the end of the 2018 season. The Patriots had been a pass-first team, and in the regular season they used
[21 personnel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-21-personnel) (two backs, with fullback James Develin) on
`{python} pct(P21["NE"])` of their snaps, second-most in the league. In the playoffs they leaned on it: 156, 177 and
156 rushing yards in their three games, with the rookie Sony Michel carrying the load, against a Chargers defense
that played light, smaller personnel, a Chiefs defense that couldn't tackle, and the Rams. The 41-year-old
Tom Brady threw less, and the team won the Super Bowl anyway. Even the weather got a game plan: in a December 2008 game
in Buffalo, in heavy wind, the Patriots ran `{python} BUF08[1]` times and threw `{python} BUF08[0]` passes, and in a
December 2021 Monday-night game in Buffalo (told in [08-03](../08-the-chess-match/08-03-game-planning-week.qmd)) they threw
three.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden, a team's offense is its playbook: pick "Spread" or "Pro Style" and that's who you are. Real NFL offenses
carry a far bigger playbook than any one game uses, and each week's [game plan](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-game-plan)
selects a slice of it for this opponent. The Patriots took that further than anyone: their system was a *language*
(Erhardt-Perkins concepts that work from any formation) rather than a list of plays, so the slice could be almost
anything. Fifty-four passes one week, thirty-nine runs the next, from the same quarterback and the same play-caller,
Josh McDaniels, is not a team with an identity crisis. It's a team whose identity is the game plan.
:::

## Situational mastery

The third leg of Belichick's football was the one fans noticed least until the last two minutes: treating every
*situation* (the end of a half, a lead to protect, fourth-and-short, a strange rule) as something to be studied and
rehearsed in advance, like an opponent. Most of the plays below are told in full in
[The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd);
put them side by side and they show a habit rather than a string of lucky calls.

- **Super Bowl XXXVI, 1:21 left, no timeouts, tied, own 17.** John Madden, on the broadcast, said New England should
  kneel and play for overtime. Belichick and Brady judged that short, safe throws to the sideline and the middle could
  move into field-goal range without risking a turnover, and that the Rams' prevent-style defense would give them
  exactly that. Nine plays, 53 yards, Vinatieri from 48 as time expired. The decision was made before the season, in
  the sense that the two-minute offense had been practiced for exactly this.
- **November 2003 at Denver, trailing.** Pinned at their own 1 with under three minutes left, down a point, the
  Patriots took an *intentional safety* to punt from the 20 instead of their own end zone, gave up two points, and won
  the game when the field position paid off.
- **Super Bowl XLVI, February 2012, leading 17–15.** With the Giants inside the 10 and about a minute left, Belichick
  told his defense to let Ahmad Bradshaw score, so that Brady would get the ball back with time. (Bradshaw tried to stop
  at the 1 and fell into the end zone; the Patriots lost anyway, but the logic was right.)
- **The 2009 fourth-and-2** at Indianapolis, told in [11-04](../11-history/11-04-dynasties-and-counterpunches.qmd): the
  analytics favoured going for it, the outcome didn't, and the decision was defensible.
- **The rulebook as a playbook.** In the January 2015 playoff game against Baltimore, the Patriots used the rules for
  reporting eligibility: a running back reported as ineligible and lined up where a receiver would stand, while a
  tight end, eligible, stood at left tackle. The Ravens couldn't sort out who could catch a pass; their coach, John
  Harbaugh, came onto the field to protest and drew a penalty; and for 2015 the league changed the rule
  ([02-02](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) explains it).
- **Super Bowl XLIX,** above: a coach who let the clock run because he liked his defensive personnel more than he wanted
  the seconds.

Is "situational mastery" real, or is it a story told about a team with a great quarterback? Some of it is measurable.[^fp]
In 2001–2019 regular seasons the Patriots outscored opponents by `{python} f"{FP_HALF['NE']:.2f}"` points per game
in the last two minutes of the first half alone, second in the league over those nineteen seasons (behind
Pittsburgh). That's the "double score" habit: points just before halftime, then, if you deferred the opening coin
toss, the ball again just after it. And in one-score games (decided by eight points or fewer) they went
`{python} NE_CLOSE_W`–`{python} NE_CLOSE_N - NE_CLOSE_W`, a `{python} f"{CLOSE_PCT['NE']:.3f}"` winning percentage, the
best in the league over the same seasons. Close-game records carry a lot of luck, and some of New England's came from
having Tom Brady. But nineteen years of them is a long streak of luck.

## The data fingerprint

If game-plan defense is real, it should leave marks in the data that a system defense wouldn't. @fig-fingerprint
tests three of them for every team, over the nineteen regular seasons from 2001 to 2019.

```{python}
#| label: fig-fingerprint
#| fig-cap: "A Belichick-era fingerprint: every NFL team, 2001-2019 regular seasons (nflverse play-by-play), New England in blue. Top: how many points opponents scored against this defense, compared with what the same opponent scored in its other games that season (negative is better). Middle: the opponent's top receiver (most receiving yards in his team's other games that season), and his share of his team's targets against this defense, minus his share in the other games. Most defenses barely change it; New England cut it the most. Bottom: point margin per game in the last two minutes of the first half."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(6.2, 4.4))
panels = [(FP_PTS, "Opponents' points vs. their own average (per game)", "{:+.1f}", "pts"),
          (FP_TOP * 100, "Opponent's top receiver: change in target share (percentage points)", "{:+.1f}", "pp"),
          (FP_HALF, "Point margin per game, last two minutes of the first half", "{:+.2f}", "pts")]
for ax, (ser, title, fmt, unit) in zip(axes, panels):
    others = ser.drop("NE")
    ax.scatter(others.values, np.zeros(len(others)), s=26, color=style.BASELINE, alpha=0.9, lw=0, zorder=2)
    ax.scatter([ser["NE"]], [0], s=60, color=style.SERIES[0], zorder=3)
    ax.annotate("NE " + fmt.format(ser["NE"]), (ser["NE"], 0), xytext=(0, 9), textcoords="offset points",
                ha="center", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
    best = ser.drop("NE").idxmin() if ser is not FP_HALF else ser.drop("NE").idxmax()
    ax.annotate(best, (ser[best], 0), xytext=(0, -13), textcoords="offset points", ha="center", fontsize=6.8,
                color=style.INK_2)
    ax.axvline(0, color=style.MUTED, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=1)
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_ylim(-1, 1)
    ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.5)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.3, loc="left", fontweight="normal", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.0)
plt.show()
```

Read it as three separate claims, each with its own caveat.

- **Opponents scored less against New England than they did against everyone else**, by
  `{python} f"{-FP_PTS['NE']:.1f}"` points a game, the biggest gap in the league (Baltimore and Pittsburgh, the era's
  great system defenses, are right behind). That's the plainest measure of a good defense, adjusted for who it played;
  it doesn't by itself prove *game-plan* defense. An offense that holds the ball for long drives also lowers the other
  team's scoring.
- **The opponent's best receiver got less of the ball.** Over these seasons a team's top receiver drew about
  `{python} pct(TOP_SHARE)` of its targets. Against most defenses, that share hardly moved. Against New England it fell
  by `{python} f"{-FP_TOP['NE'] * 100:.1f}"` percentage points, the largest drop of any defense and about three times the
  next team's. That's small per game (a target or so) but it is exactly the fingerprint Lombardi's line predicts:
  a defense that aims at "what their individual players do best" should push the ball away from the opponent's best
  player, and this one did, for nineteen years.
- **The end of the half belonged to the Patriots.** The situational habit shows up as almost a point a game in a
  two-minute window, second only to Pittsburgh.

None of these is enormous, and none should be: they're averages over hundreds of games against every kind of
opponent. What's striking is that one team sits at or near the end of all three lines.

## How opponents responded

Every scheme in this course creates its own counter, and Belichick's had several.

**Make the plan irrelevant with four rushers.** The two teams that beat Brady and Belichick in Super Bowls in the
2000s, the 2007 and 2011 Giants, did it the way [11-04](../11-history/11-04-dynasties-and-counterpunches.qmd)
describes: a four-man rush good enough to reach Brady without blitzing, with linemen pushing up the middle where a
pocket passer can't escape. A game plan on offense can hide a weakness from a coordinator, but not from four
defensive linemen who win their matchups on every play. The 2015 Denver defense did it again in the AFC Championship
Game, hitting Brady over and over.[^den15]
<!-- VERIFY: count of hits on Brady in the January 24, 2016 AFC Championship Game (often reported as 20, a season high for any QB that year). -->

**Have too many best things.** A plan that takes one thing away works best against an offense with one thing. The
2017 Eagles in Super Bowl LII spread the ball among receivers, tight ends and backs, and their backup quarterback
played the game of his life; there was no single target to take away. The great quarterbacks who beat New England,
Peyton Manning in the 2006 and 2015 AFC title games, later Patrick Mahomes, could beat a defense "left-handed",
throwing to whoever was left.

**Take away *their* best thing.** Defenses turned the method around: bracket Gronkowski, double Welker, press
Edelman, and dare the second and third options to win. The Patriots' answer, again and again, was to change which
player was the best thing that week.

**Hire his assistants.** The most direct response was to hire the people who knew how the plans were built. Romeo
Crennel, Nick Saban (the Browns' defensive coordinator under Belichick), Eric Mangini, Charlie Weis, Josh McDaniels,
Bill O'Brien, Matt Patricia, Brian Flores and Mike Vrabel all became head coaches. Their records were mixed, which is
itself a lesson: the plans came from a *process* (the film work, the weekly installs, the players chosen to absorb
them), and a coordinator who leaves takes the habits but not the building.

## What survives

Almost all of it, and much of it has become ordinary.

- **Every defense game-plans now.** Weekly, opponent-specific defense was Belichick's signature in 2001. By 2026 it
  is simply how the league works: coordinators build a [disguise](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)
  package and a set of matchup rules for each opponent, and the rise of two-high,
  rotate-at-the-snap defenses ([The Modern Era](../11-history/11-05-the-modern-era.qmd)) is the LIII plan as a
  league-wide style: show one picture, play another. The clearest recent example sits on the other sideline from
  New England. In Super Bowl LX in February 2026, Mike Macdonald's Seattle defense sacked Drake Maye six times and
  beat the Patriots 29–13. New England's head coach that night was Mike Vrabel, a linebacker on Belichick's first
  three Super Bowl teams, with Josh McDaniels calling the offense.[^lx] (Macdonald's defense gets its own case study in
  [From Two-High to Macdonald](12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd).)
- **Versatile players over specialists.** Defensive backs who can play corner, safety and slot; linebackers who rush
  and drop; tight ends who block and run routes. A game plan is only as flexible as the players who have to learn it,
  and Belichick's roster-building made that the priority it is now.
- **Situational football as a subject.** Teams now carry analysts for fourth-down, two-point and clock decisions (see
  [Win Probability and Fourth Downs](../13-analytics-and-data/13-03-win-probability-and-fourth-down.qmd)), and practise
  end-of-half and end-of-game situations weekly.
- **Concept language.** The Erhardt-Perkins way of naming plays (concepts, not formations) survives in many offenses,
  including McDaniels's in New England in 2026.

Belichick left New England after the 2023 season. He became head coach at the University of North Carolina for the
2025 season, which ended 4–8, and in January 2026, in his first year of eligibility, he was not elected to the Pro
Football Hall of Fame, a vote that drew wide criticism.[^unc] One of his game plans is there already: the
handwritten Super Bowl XXV sheets.

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: the take-away test"}
Pick one game. Before kickoff, write down the answer to Belichick's first question for **each** offense: what does
it most need? A player (its star receiver, its running back), a concept (play-action off the run, the quick game), or
a part of the field (the deep middle, the perimeter run)?

**Early in the game,** watch the defense on that team's first few snaps:

- Where is the star? Is a second defender near him (a safety over the top, a corner outside, a linebacker underneath)?
  That's a bracket, a take-away.
- How many defenders stand on the line before the snap, and how many actually rush? A defense with six on the line and
  four rushers is hiding something.
- Does the coverage look the same before and after the snap? If the picture changes, the defense is disguising: it's
  aiming at the quarterback's pre-snap read.

**At halftime and at the end,** check your note. Did the star get his usual share of targets or carries? Who got the
ball instead? Was the thing the defense conceded (the run? the short throw? the other receiver?) the thing that beat
it, or the thing it could live with? A defense that "gave up" 120 rushing yards and won may have been paying a bill it
chose on Wednesday.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: the key, turned around"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-key
#| fig-cap: "Third quarter, second-and-6 near midfield. All game this defense has keyed on the running back's alignment, the way New England did against Faulk: back directly behind the quarterback means run, back offset means pass. Against an offset back it has been in dime (six defensive backs, one linebacker, M), pressing the receivers, with the end on the back's side (E, purple ring) crashing on him whenever he releases. The offense lines up with its back offset again (R, red ring), the same look as on the pass plays."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", UC, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 2.8, "R"), O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0),
                 O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8), O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -9.0), O("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 15.0)]
p = Play(off, pats_dime_press(), los=own(48), to_go=6)
p.highlight("RB", color=RED)
p.highlight("RDE", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-18.5, 18.5), window=(-8.5, 15.5), width_in=5.6)
point_to(f, p, (-7.0, 9.6), (-5.0, 2.8), "R offset again", color=OD)
say(f, p, 9.0, -9.0, "dime: one linebacker\nin the box", fontsize=6.5, color=DD)
say(f, p, 3.0, -15.4, "press", fontsize=6.2, color=DD)
say(f, p, 3.0, 15.4, "press", fontsize=6.2, color=DD)
plt.show()
```

**The defense has been right all game about what the offset back means. What should the offense call now, and why?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A run from the pass look: a draw or an inside run, or a screen to the back that uses the end's crash against
him.** Every key a defense uses is a [tendency](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tendency) the offense can scout,
and once the offense knows the defense trusts it, the key becomes a lever (the
[tendency breaker](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tendency-breaker) of
[Constraint Theory](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd)). Look at what the key has
bought the defense: six defensive backs and one linebacker, corners pressed on the outside, an end flying upfield.
That's a light box. A draw, with the linemen showing pass and then blocking the rushers where they've chosen to go,
puts the back against one linebacker and a safety. A screen to his side lets the crashing end run himself out of the
play.

Two notes. On second-and-6 a 4-yard run is a fine result, so the offense isn't risking much by testing the key. And
the defense's coaches know this too. A good game-plan defense keeps the key for most of the game and then *shows* the
key while playing something else, a base front against the offset back, say, on the down it expects the
tendency breaker. That's why Belichick's 2001 staff changed so much between the regular-season meeting and the
Super Bowl: they expected the Rams to adjust to what they'd seen in November.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: frozen in nickel"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-freeze
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-4, first quarter. On first down the offense had two tight ends on the field, its star tight end (Y, red ring) split out wide, and the defense substituted to nickel to cover him (the nickel back, $, purple ring). Now the offense has hurried to the line without a huddle, so the defense can't change personnel, and it has lined up tight: both tight ends attached to the line and a back seven yards deep."
off = pats12(y_w=4.8, u_w=-4.8, z_w=13.0, x_w=-15.0)
dfn = dl4() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 1.2, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.8, "W"), D("NB", "NB", 4.0, 7.6, "$"),
               D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.0, 13.0, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 9.0, -6.0, "SS"),
               D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 3.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=own(40), to_go=4)
p.highlight("Y", color=RED)
p.highlight("NB", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-18.0, 18.0), window=(-9.0, 15.5), width_in=5.6)
say(f, p, -4.6, 9.8, "no huddle: the defense\ncan't substitute", fontsize=6.5, color=OD)
point_to(f, p, (9.0, 10.6), (4.0, 7.6), "a 190-pound nickel\nback on the edge", color=DD)
plt.show()
```

**What's the offense going to do, and why did it skip the huddle?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Run right, at the nickel back, with the star tight end blocking him.** This is the dilemma from @fig-gronk with
[tempo](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tempo) added. First down was the question: what do you do when our tight
end splits out? The defense answered by sending on a nickel back, a defensive back of about 190 pounds, in place of
a linebacker. Now the offense has kept the same eleven players, lined up as a running formation, and snapped the ball
before the defense could send its linebacker back on; a no-huddle offense that never substitutes can hold a defense in
the wrong personnel, the [substitution freeze](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-substitution-freeze) of
[In-Game Adjustments](../08-the-chess-match/08-04-in-game-adjustments-and-tempo.qmd). The defense has seven players
near the line against seven blockers plus the back, and its edge player on the right is the smallest man on the
field, facing a 265-pound tight end. That's a run play's dream.

If the defense keeps answering with base personnel instead, the offense splits the tight end out again and throws
at the linebacker. The table in Panel D of @fig-gronk is the whole game. (The Patriots of 2011–2012 played this way
for long stretches; 11-04 has their 2012 total of 1,191 offensive plays.)
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: fifty-eight seconds"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-half
#| fig-cap: "Second quarter, 0:58 left, tied 10–10. The offense has the ball first-and-10 at its own 30 with two timeouts, and it will receive the second-half kickoff (it won the coin toss and deferred). The defense has gone to a soft two-deep shell: two safeties deep, the corners off, linebackers and the nickel dropping to the sticks."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, 1.7, "R"), O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -16.0),
                 O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -9.0), O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 8.0), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 16.0)]
dfn = dl4() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 6.5, -1.5, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 6.5, 3.5, "W"), D("NB", "NB", 6.0, -9.0, "$"),
               D("LCB", "CB", 8.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 8.0, 16.0, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 18.0, 9.0, "SS"),
               D("FS", "FS", 18.0, -9.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=own(30), to_go=10)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-20.0, 20.0), window=(-9.5, 22.0), width_in=5.6)
x0, y0 = P(f, p, -6.0, -17.6)
f.ax.text(float(x0), float(y0), "Q2  0:58   10–10\nown 30, 1st & 10\n2 timeouts left\nreceive 2nd-half kick",
          fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK, va="center", ha="left", zorder=14, linespacing=1.2,
          bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.35", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8))
say(f, p, 13.5, 0.0, "soft: everything\nin front of them", fontsize=6.5, color=DD)
plt.show()
```

**Many coaches would kneel and take the tie into halftime. What did Belichick's teams usually do here, and why?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Attack, carefully: throw underneath the soft shell, get out of bounds or use a timeout after each completion, and
aim for field-goal range.** The arithmetic is the "double score" from
[The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd).
Fifty-eight seconds and two timeouts is enough for four to six plays. A defense playing this deep gives away 8- to
12-yard throws in front of it, and two or three of those reach the opponent's 35, a long but makeable field goal.
Then, because this offense deferred the coin toss, it gets the ball again to start the second half. Two possessions
in a row, separated only by halftime, can turn a tie into a 10-point lead in a few minutes of game time.

The risk is a turnover deep in your own territory, which is why the throws are short, the sideline is used, and
nothing goes up for grabs; if the first two plays go nowhere, the right call becomes the kneel. The Patriots made this
sequence a habit. In 2001–2019 they outscored opponents by `{python} f"{FP_HALF['NE']:.2f}"` points a game in the last
two minutes of the first half, second in the league (@fig-fingerprint). It's the same thinking as Super Bowl XXXVI's
last drive, from your own 17 with no timeouts: a situation rehearsed in practice is a situation you can attack.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **A game-plan defense chooses its weakness every week.** Eleven defenders can't stop everything, so Belichick's
  defenses asked what *this* offense most needed, took that away, and named in advance what they'd concede. The
  concession is part of the plan, not a failure of it.
- **The target is usually a person.** Kelly's passing (and Thomas as a receiver) in Super Bowl XXV, Marshall Faulk in
  XXXVI, Goff's pre-snap read in LIII. In 2001–2019 data, the opponent's top receiver lost more of his share of the
  targets against New England than against any other defense.
- **Each plan looked nothing like the last.** Two linemen and six defensive backs; a defense keyed on one running
  back's alignment; six on the line with zone behind after a season of man. What repeated was the method: three
  questions, asked fresh each week.
- **The offense was a chameleon for the same reason.** A concept language that works from any formation let the
  Patriots throw 54 times one playoff week and run 39 times the next, and turn Gronkowski into a personnel dilemma
  the defense had to solve before seeing the formation.
- **Situations were rehearsed like opponents.** End-of-half drives, intentional safeties, letting a team score, the
  eligibility rules, the clock at the end of Super Bowl XLIX: the Patriots treated each as something to prepare, and the
  close-game and end-of-half numbers show it.
- **Super Bowl XLIX was decided by preparation, not by the call.** A defensible pass met a jam and a jumped slant
  that New England had rehearsed that week against that formation.

[^fp]: Course calculations from nflverse play-by-play, 2001–2019 regular seasons. End-of-half margin: points scored

    team's points in a game minus its average in its other games that season. Top receiver: the receiver with the most
    receiving yards in his team's other games that season (at least six other games), his share of the team's targets
    in this game minus his share in the other games; games he missed are excluded.
